about: Topic map of the AP Chemistry Course and Exam Description (Fall 2024 revision), written in LevlPrep's own words from docs/apchem-research/framework.md. No CED text is reproduced. Objectives and knowledge are paraphrases for authors; exclusions for Units 1-2 were read in the CED, those for Units 3-9 are reported by secondary sources and must be verified (docs/apchem-needs-author.md, ced-exclusions).

ced.title: AP Chemistry Course and Exam Description
ced.verification: The CED PDF text was read through topic 3.1; topic lists for all units were read from the CED and the Course at a Glance. Exclusions after 3.1 come from secondary sources.
ced.oldNamesWarning: Do not copy unit names or topic numbers from pre-2024 resources (old 7.13 is now 8.11, old 7.14 is now 9.6, old 9.6-9.10 are now 9.7-9.11).

sciencePracticesNote: MCQ assesses practices 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6; practice 3 is free response only. Weights by practice are from third-party copies of the CED exam table [unverified].

topics.title: Moles and Molar Mass
objectives: Connect the number of particles, the amount in moles and the mass of a sample.
knowledge: Chemists count particles in moles because single atoms and molecules are far too small to count or weigh.
One mole is 6.022 × 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number).
The mass of one particle in atomic mass units has the same number as the mass of one mole in grams (the molar mass).
Dimensional analysis moves between mass, moles and number of particles.

topics.title: Mass Spectra of Elements
objectives: Explain how a mass spectrum shows an element's isotopes and their abundances, and find the average atomic mass from it.
knowledge: Atoms of one element all have the same number of protons but can differ in neutrons: these are isotopes.
A mass spectrometer separates singly charged ions by mass; each peak is one isotope and its height is the relative abundance.
The average atomic mass on the periodic table is the abundance-weighted average of the isotope masses.
exclusions: Mass spectra of samples with more than one element, and peaks from anything other than singly charged ions of single atoms, are not tested.

topics.title: Elemental Composition of Pure Substances
objectives: Relate the mass percent of each element in a pure compound to its empirical formula.
knowledge: A pure compound always has the same elements in the same mass proportions (law of definite proportions).
Mass percent of an element = mass of that element in the formula ÷ molar mass × 100.
The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; find it from mass data by converting to moles and dividing by the smallest.
The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, found with the molar mass.

topics.title: Composition of Mixtures
objectives: Explain how the composition of a mixture can vary, and use elemental analysis to find the purity of a sample.
knowledge: A mixture contains two or more substances whose proportions can vary; a pure substance has fixed composition.
Homogeneous mixtures have uniform composition; heterogeneous mixtures do not.
Elemental analysis (for example, mass percent of one element) can show how pure a sample is or what it is mixed with.
Particulate diagrams show substances at the level of particles; the macroscopic level is what we see and measure.

topics.title: Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration
objectives: Write the electron configuration of an atom or ion and explain electron energies with Coulomb's law.
knowledge: Coulomb's law: the attraction between the nucleus and an electron grows with the charges and falls with distance.
Electrons occupy shells and subshells (s, p, d) filled in order of increasing energy (aufbau principle).
Electrons in the outermost shell are valence electrons; inner (core) electrons shield valence electrons from the nucleus.
Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron; it reflects how strongly the nucleus holds it.
exclusions: Assigning quantum numbers to electrons is not tested.

topics.title: Photoelectron Spectroscopy
objectives: Read a photoelectron spectrum to identify an element's electron configuration and compare electron energies.
knowledge: Photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) uses high-energy light to knock electrons out and measures the energy each needed (binding energy).
Each peak is one subshell; its position gives the binding energy and its relative height gives the number of electrons.
Electrons closer to the nucleus (lower shells) have higher binding energies; a larger nuclear charge raises every peak.

topics.title: Periodic Trends
objectives: Explain trends in atomic radius, ionization energy, electronegativity and electron affinity with Coulomb's law and shielding.
knowledge: Across a period, nuclear charge rises while shielding barely changes, so atoms get smaller and hold electrons more tightly.
Down a group, electrons occupy more shells, so atoms get larger and hold valence electrons less tightly.
Electronegativity is how strongly an atom attracts shared electrons; it rises across a period and falls down a group.
Trends are explained by number of protons, distance and shielding, not by "wanting" a full octet.
exclusions: Writing electron configurations for elements that break the aufbau order is not tested.

topics.title: Valence Electrons and Ionic Compounds
objectives: Predict the charges of common ions and the formulas of ionic compounds from valence electrons.
knowledge: Main-group atoms tend to gain or lose valence electrons until they have the electron configuration of a noble gas.
Metals form cations; nonmetals form anions; the charges must add to zero in an ionic compound.
Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of valence electrons.

topics.title: Types of Chemical Bonds
objectives: Classify bonds as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, ionic or metallic from electronegativity and the elements involved.
knowledge: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons; unequal sharing between atoms of different electronegativity makes it polar.
An ionic bond is the Coulombic attraction between cations and anions, typically a metal with a nonmetal.
Metallic bonding is cations held in a sea of delocalized valence electrons.
Bond character is a continuum: a larger electronegativity difference means more polar, more ionic character.

topics.title: Intramolecular Force and Potential Energy
objectives: Explain the shape of a potential energy curve for two bonded atoms and relate bond length and bond energy to it.
knowledge: As two atoms approach, attraction lowers the potential energy until repulsion between nuclei makes it rise again.
The minimum of the curve gives the bond length and its depth gives the bond energy.
Double and triple bonds are shorter and stronger than single bonds between the same atoms.
For ions, Coulomb's law shows that larger charges and smaller ions give stronger attraction.

topics.title: Structure of Ionic Solids
objectives: Explain the properties of ionic solids from the arrangement of ions and Coulombic attractions.
knowledge: Ionic solids are a repeating three-dimensional array of alternating cations and anions.
Strong attractions throughout the lattice give high melting points and brittleness.
Ionic solids do not conduct electricity, but melted or dissolved, their ions can move and they conduct.
exclusions: Knowledge of specific crystal structures is not tested.

topics.title: Structure of Metals and Alloys
objectives: Explain the properties of metals and alloys from metallic bonding and the sizes of the atoms involved.
knowledge: Delocalized electrons let metals conduct electricity and heat, and let layers slide, so metals are malleable and ductile.
In an interstitial alloy, small atoms fill holes between larger metal atoms, making the metal harder and less malleable.
In a substitutional alloy, atoms of similar size replace metal atoms in the lattice.

topics.title: Lewis Diagrams
objectives: Draw Lewis diagrams for molecules and polyatomic ions from valence electron counts.
knowledge: A Lewis diagram shows every valence electron as bonding pairs (lines) and lone pairs (dots).
Most second-period atoms end with eight electrons around them (octet rule); hydrogen ends with two.
Some molecules break the octet rule: incomplete octets (B), odd electron counts, and expanded octets from period 3 on.

topics.title: Resonance and Formal Charge
objectives: Draw resonance structures and use formal charge to choose the best Lewis diagram.
knowledge: When more than one valid Lewis diagram exists, the real structure is a resonance hybrid of them; electrons are delocalized.
Formal charge = valence electrons − lone-pair electrons − half the bonding electrons.
The best diagram has formal charges closest to zero, with any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom.
Resonance gives equal, intermediate bond lengths and fractional bond orders.

topics.title: VSEPR and Hybridization
objectives: Predict molecular geometry, bond angles, polarity and hybridization from a Lewis diagram.
knowledge: Electron domains (bonds and lone pairs) around a central atom spread out as far apart as possible (VSEPR).
Lone pairs take up more room than bonding pairs and squeeze bond angles.
A molecule is polar when its bond dipoles do not cancel because of its shape.
Hybridization (sp, sp², sp³) matches the number of electron domains; single bonds are sigma bonds, and each extra bond in a double or triple bond is a pi bond.
exclusions: Deriving or drawing hybrid orbitals, hybridization involving d orbitals, and molecular orbital theory are not tested.

topics.title: Intermolecular and Interparticle Forces
objectives: Identify the forces between particles of a substance and use them to compare physical properties.
knowledge: London dispersion forces exist between all particles and grow with the number of electrons (polarizability), not with mass as such.
Polar molecules also attract by dipole-dipole forces; hydrogen bonds form when H bonded to N, O or F meets a lone pair on N, O or F.
Ion-dipole forces hold ions and polar molecules together, as when salts dissolve in water.
Stronger forces between particles mean higher boiling and melting points and lower vapor pressure.
Intermolecular forces are much weaker than the bonds inside molecules; boiling breaks no covalent bonds.
exclusions: Note: London dispersion forces are not another name for all van der Waals forces.

topics.title: Properties of Solids
objectives: Classify solids as ionic, molecular, covalent network or metallic and explain their properties.
knowledge: Molecular solids are held by intermolecular forces, so they melt low and do not conduct.
Covalent network solids (diamond, quartz) are one continuous web of covalent bonds: very high melting points, very hard.
Crystalline solids have an ordered repeating arrangement; amorphous solids do not.

topics.title: Solids, Liquids, and Gases
objectives: Describe the arrangement and motion of particles in each phase and explain phase changes and vapor pressure.
knowledge: Particles in a solid vibrate in place; in a liquid they are close but move past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move freely.
A phase change rearranges particles by overcoming or forming intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.
In a closed container, evaporation and condensation reach a dynamic equilibrium; the gas pressure then is the vapor pressure.
A liquid has a vapor pressure at every temperature, not only at its boiling point.

topics.title: Ideal Gas Law
objectives: Use the ideal gas law and Dalton's law to relate pressure, volume, temperature and amount of gas.
knowledge: PV = nRT links the four gas variables; T must be in kelvin and R must match the pressure and volume units.
The combined gas law relates two states of the same gas sample.
In a mixture, each gas has a partial pressure; they add to the total pressure, and the mole fraction gives each share.
Molar mass and density of a gas can be found from PV = nRT.

topics.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory
objectives: Explain gas behavior with the kinetic molecular theory and read Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions.
knowledge: Gas particles move randomly, collide elastically, and take up negligible volume compared with the container.
Average kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature; at the same temperature, lighter particles move faster.
A Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shows the spread of particle speeds; raising the temperature flattens it and shifts it to higher speeds.

topics.title: Deviation from Ideal Gas Law
objectives: Explain when and why real gases deviate from ideal behavior.
knowledge: Real gases deviate most at high pressure and low temperature, and for particles with strong intermolecular forces or large volumes.
Attractions between particles make the measured pressure lower than ideal; particle volume makes the real volume larger than ideal.

topics.title: Solutions and Mixtures
objectives: Calculate molarity, prepare solutions and dilutions, and describe solutions at the particle level.
knowledge: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent; in an aqueous solution the solvent is water.
Molarity = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution (not liters of solvent).
Dilution: moles of solute stay the same, so M1V1 = M2V2; V2 is the total final volume.
Prepare a solution precisely with an analytical balance and a volumetric flask filled to the mark.
exclusions: Molality, percent by mass and percent by volume calculations of solutions, and colligative properties, are reported as not tested (needs-author: verify against the CED).

topics.title: Representations of Solutions
objectives: Draw and read particle diagrams of solutions, with ions and water molecules correctly placed and oriented.
knowledge: When an ionic solid dissolves, its ions separate (dissociate) and are surrounded by water molecules (hydration).
Water's partially negative oxygen points toward cations; its partially positive hydrogens point toward anions.
A particle diagram of a solution keeps the formula ratio of ions and shows solute particles spread evenly.

topics.title: Separation of Solutions and Mixtures
objectives: Explain how chromatography and distillation separate components by their intermolecular interactions.
knowledge: In chromatography, components that interact more strongly with the stationary phase move more slowly; Rf compares distance traveled.
Distillation separates liquids because the one with weaker intermolecular forces has the higher vapor pressure and boils first.
Filtration separates an undissolved solid from a liquid.

topics.title: Solubility
objectives: Predict and explain solubility from the interactions between solute and solvent particles.
knowledge: A substance dissolves well when solute-solvent attractions are similar in strength to the attractions they replace ("like dissolves like").
Polar and ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents; nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents.
Gas solubility in water rises with gas pressure and falls as temperature rises.

topics.title: Spectroscopy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
objectives: Match regions of the electromagnetic spectrum to the molecular and electronic changes they cause.
knowledge: Microwaves change rotational energy, infrared changes vibrational energy, and ultraviolet and visible light move electrons between energy levels.
Absorption happens only when a photon's energy matches the difference between two energy levels.

topics.title: Properties of Photons
objectives: Calculate the energy, frequency and wavelength of light and relate them to energy level differences.
knowledge: Light travels at c = λν, so frequency and wavelength are inversely related.
A photon's energy is E = hν; higher frequency (shorter wavelength) means more energy.
Energy per photon in joules converts to energy per mole with Avogadro's number.

topics.title: Beer-Lambert Law
objectives: Use the Beer-Lambert law and a calibration curve to find concentration from absorbance.
knowledge: Absorbance is proportional to concentration, path length and molar absorptivity: A = εbc.
Measure at the wavelength of maximum absorbance; a calibration curve of standards gives concentration from absorbance.
Errors such as fingerprints on the cuvette or a wrong blank change the absorbance read and the concentration found.

topics.title: Introduction for Reactions
objectives: Recognize evidence of a chemical reaction and write balanced chemical equations.
knowledge: In a chemical reaction atoms rearrange into new substances; atoms are conserved, so equations must balance.
Evidence can include a color change, a gas, a precipitate or a temperature change, but none of these alone proves a reaction.
Coefficients give mole ratios; subscripts are fixed by the formulas and never changed to balance.

topics.title: Net Ionic Equations
objectives: Write net ionic equations that show only the species that change.
knowledge: Strong electrolytes are written as separate ions; solids, liquids, gases and weak electrolytes stay as formulas.
Spectator ions appear unchanged on both sides and are left out of the net ionic equation.
A net ionic equation must balance both atoms and charge.

topics.title: Representations of Reactions
objectives: Move between balanced equations and particle diagrams of a reaction.
knowledge: A particle diagram of a reaction conserves every atom and shows the ratio given by the coefficients.
State symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) say how each species exists.
Leftover reactant particles in a diagram show which reactant was in excess.

topics.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
objectives: Distinguish physical from chemical changes by what happens to particles and bonds.
knowledge: A physical change alters arrangement or phase without making new substances; a chemical change forms new substances with new bonds.
Dissolving an ionic solid breaks ionic attractions and forms ion-dipole attractions, so it has features of both.

topics.title: Stoichiometry
objectives: Use mole ratios from a balanced equation to find amounts of reactants and products, including the limiting reactant.
knowledge: Mole ratios from coefficients convert moles of one species into moles of another.
The limiting reactant runs out first and sets the theoretical yield; the other reactant is in excess.
Percent yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.
Gravimetric analysis finds the amount of an ion from the mass of a precipitate.

topics.title: Introduction to Titration
objectives: Find an unknown concentration from titration data at the equivalence point.
knowledge: In a titration, a solution of known concentration (titrant) is added from a buret to the analyte until they have reacted in stoichiometric amounts.
At the equivalence point, moles of titrant added match the moles of analyte by the mole ratio.
An indicator changes color at the end point, which should be close to the equivalence point.
Rinse the buret with the titrant, read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus, and record to the right precision.

topics.title: Types of Chemical Reactions
objectives: Classify reactions as precipitation, acid-base, redox or combustion and predict products.
knowledge: Precipitation reactions form an insoluble solid from two solutions.
Acid-base reactions transfer a proton; redox reactions transfer electrons.
Combustion of a hydrocarbon in excess oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water.

topics.title: Introduction to Acid-Base Reactions
objectives: Identify Brønsted-Lowry acids, bases and conjugate pairs in a proton-transfer reaction.
knowledge: A Brønsted-Lowry acid donates a proton (H⁺); a base accepts one.
Removing H⁺ from an acid gives its conjugate base; adding H⁺ to a base gives its conjugate acid.
Water is amphoteric: it can act as an acid or a base; in water, H⁺ exists as hydronium, H₃O⁺.

topics.title: Oxidation-Reduction (Redox) Reactions
objectives: Assign oxidation numbers, identify what is oxidized and reduced, and balance redox reactions with half-reactions.
knowledge: Oxidation is loss of electrons (oxidation number rises); reduction is gain of electrons (oxidation number falls).
The oxidizing agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidized.
Balance a redox reaction by writing half-reactions so that electrons lost equal electrons gained.

topics.title: Reaction Rates
objectives: Express reaction rates from concentration changes and relate rates of different species through the balanced equation.
knowledge: Rate is the change in concentration per unit time; it can be measured by any species.
Rates of appearance and disappearance are related by the coefficients of the balanced equation.
Rates depend on concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts.

topics.title: Introduction to Rate Law
objectives: Determine a rate law and rate constant from initial-rate data.
knowledge: A rate law has the form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n; the orders m and n come from experiment, not from coefficients.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes to find each order.
The units of k depend on the overall order.

topics.title: Concentration Changes Over Time
objectives: Use integrated rate laws, linear plots and half-life to find order and rate constants.
knowledge: First order: a plot of ln[A] against time is linear with slope −k; second order: 1/[A] against time is linear with slope k; zero order: [A] against time is linear.
Name the plot that is linear when you justify an order.
A first-order reaction has a constant half-life, t½ = 0.693/k, independent of concentration.

topics.title: Elementary Reactions
objectives: Write the rate law of an elementary reaction from its molecularity.
knowledge: An elementary reaction happens in a single collision or event; its rate law follows directly from its coefficients.
Molecularity is the number of particles colliding: unimolecular, bimolecular, rarely termolecular.

topics.title: Collision Model
objectives: Explain reaction rates with collision frequency, energy and orientation.
knowledge: A reaction happens only when particles collide with enough energy (the activation energy) and the right orientation.
Raising the temperature increases collision frequency and, much more, the fraction of collisions with enough energy.
On a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, the area beyond the activation energy is the fraction of particles that can react.

topics.title: Reaction Energy Profile
objectives: Read and draw a reaction energy profile and relate it to rate.
knowledge: An energy profile plots potential energy along the reaction coordinate from reactants through the transition state to products.
The activation energy is the rise from reactants to the transition state; the overall energy change is products minus reactants.
A larger activation energy gives a smaller rate constant at the same temperature.

topics.title: Introduction to Reaction Mechanisms
objectives: Check that a mechanism adds up to the overall reaction and identify intermediates.
knowledge: A reaction mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps that adds up to the overall equation.
An intermediate is formed in one step and used up in a later step; it does not appear in the overall equation.

topics.title: Reaction Mechanism and Rate Law
objectives: Derive the rate law of a mechanism whose first step is slow.
knowledge: The slowest step (rate-determining step) limits the overall rate.
If the first step is slow, the overall rate law is the rate law of that step.
A mechanism is consistent with data only if its predicted rate law matches the experimental one.

topics.title: Pre-Equilibrium Approximation
objectives: Derive the rate law of a mechanism with a fast reversible first step followed by a slow step.
knowledge: When a fast reversible step comes before the slow step, its forward and reverse rates are equal.
Setting them equal expresses the intermediate's concentration with reactant concentrations, which removes it from the rate law.

topics.title: Multistep Reaction Energy Profile
objectives: Read a multistep energy profile to find intermediates and the rate-determining step.
knowledge: Each elementary step has its own hump; valleys between humps are intermediates.
The step with the highest transition state relative to its starting point is usually the slowest step.

topics.title: Catalysis
objectives: Explain how a catalyst speeds a reaction and distinguish a catalyst from an intermediate.
knowledge: A catalyst provides a new mechanism with a lower activation energy; it is used in one step and regenerated in a later one.
A catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions equally; it does not change the overall energy change or the equilibrium.
Catalysts can be homogeneous, heterogeneous (surface), acid-base, or enzymes.

topics.title: Endothermic and Exothermic Processes
objectives: Classify processes as endothermic or exothermic from temperature data and particle-level reasoning.
knowledge: In an exothermic process energy flows from the system to the surroundings; in an endothermic process it flows in.
A temperature rise in the surroundings (the water or calorimeter) signals an exothermic process.
Breaking attractions or bonds absorbs energy; forming them releases energy.

topics.title: Energy Diagrams
objectives: Represent energy changes with energy diagrams and connect them to the sign of ΔH.
knowledge: An energy diagram shows reactants and products at their enthalpies; the difference is ΔH.
Products lower than reactants: ΔH negative, exothermic; higher: ΔH positive, endothermic.

topics.title: Heat Transfer and Thermal Equilibrium
objectives: Explain heat transfer between objects at the particle level until thermal equilibrium.
knowledge: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, by collisions between particles.
Energy flows from the warmer object to the cooler one until they reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).
Energy lost by one object equals energy gained by the other in an isolated system.

topics.title: Heat Capacity and Calorimetry
objectives: Calculate heat with q = mcΔT and find enthalpy changes from calorimetry data.
knowledge: q = mcΔT; specific heat capacity is the energy to raise 1 g by 1 °C (or 1 K).
In a coffee-cup calorimeter, the heat released by the reaction equals the heat gained by the solution, with opposite sign.
Divide q by moles of the limiting reactant for the molar enthalpy change, with the sign set by the direction of flow.
Heat lost to the surroundings or a wrong mass or ΔT changes the result in a predictable direction.

topics.title: Energy of Phase Changes
objectives: Calculate the energy of phase changes and read heating curves.
knowledge: During a phase change, added energy overcomes intermolecular forces and the temperature stays constant.
Enthalpy of fusion and of vaporization are per mole; vaporization is larger because the forces are overcome completely.
A heating curve has sloped parts (q = mcΔT) and flat parts (q = nΔH).

topics.title: Introduction to Enthalpy of Reaction
objectives: Use the enthalpy of reaction with stoichiometry to find the heat of a reaction.
knowledge: ΔH°rxn is the enthalpy change for the reaction as written, in kJ per mole of reaction.
Heat for a given amount = moles × ΔH per the coefficients; reversing a reaction changes the sign.
The sign of q for the surroundings is opposite to that of the reaction.

topics.title: Bond Enthalpies
objectives: Estimate ΔH of reaction from bond enthalpies.
knowledge: Breaking bonds absorbs energy; forming bonds releases it.
ΔH ≈ (bonds broken) − (bonds formed), using average bond enthalpies, which makes it an estimate.

topics.title: Enthalpy of Formation
objectives: Calculate ΔH°rxn from standard enthalpies of formation.
knowledge: The standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change to make one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states.
Elements in their standard states have ΔH°f = 0.
ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f(products) − Σ ΔH°f(reactants), each times its coefficient.

topics.title: Hess's Law
objectives: Combine reactions and their enthalpies with Hess's law.
knowledge: Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH for an overall reaction is the sum of ΔH for steps that add up to it.
Reversing a step changes the sign of its ΔH; multiplying a step multiplies its ΔH.

topics.title: Introduction to Equilibrium
objectives: Describe chemical equilibrium as equal forward and reverse rates with constant concentrations.
knowledge: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant, not equal.
Equilibrium can be approached from either direction.
Concentration-time graphs level off at equilibrium.

topics.title: Direction of Reversible Reactions
objectives: Explain which way a reversible reaction proceeds from the relative forward and reverse rates.
knowledge: If the forward rate is greater than the reverse rate, the net reaction goes forward, and vice versa.
Adding or removing a species changes one rate first, so the system has a net change until rates are equal again.

topics.title: Reaction Quotient and Equilibrium Constant
objectives: Write expressions for K and Q and compare them to predict the direction of a reaction.
knowledge: K is products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient, at equilibrium; Q has the same form for any moment.
Kc uses molar concentrations; Kp uses partial pressures.
Pure solids and liquids are left out of K and Q.
Q < K: net forward; Q > K: net reverse; Q = K: at equilibrium.

topics.title: Calculating the Equilibrium Constant
objectives: Calculate K from equilibrium concentrations or pressures.
knowledge: Substitute equilibrium values into the K expression; K has no units on the exam.
Use an initial-change-equilibrium table when only some equilibrium values are given.
Heterogeneous equilibria include only gases and dissolved species in K.

topics.title: Magnitude of the Equilibrium Constant
objectives: Use the size of K to say whether reactants or products are favored at equilibrium.
knowledge: K much larger than 1: products favored at equilibrium; K much smaller than 1: reactants favored.
The size of K says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached.

topics.title: Properties of the Equilibrium Constant
objectives: Find K for reversed, multiplied or added reactions.
knowledge: Reversing a reaction gives 1/K; multiplying the equation by n raises K to the n; adding reactions multiplies their K values.
K depends only on temperature for a given reaction.

topics.title: Calculating Equilibrium Concentrations
objectives: Find equilibrium concentrations from K and initial amounts with an ICE table.
knowledge: An ICE table tracks initial amounts, the change (x times coefficients) and equilibrium amounts.
When K is small, x is small compared with the starting concentration and can be dropped from sums and differences.
Compare Q with K first to know which direction the change goes.

topics.title: Representations of Equilibrium
objectives: Read particle diagrams and graphs of systems at equilibrium and calculate K from particle counts.
knowledge: A particle diagram at equilibrium shows a mixture whose composition no longer changes over time.
Counting particles of each species (and dividing by volume) gives concentrations for K.

topics.title: Introduction to Le Châtelier's Principle
objectives: Predict how an equilibrium shifts when concentration, pressure, volume or temperature change.
knowledge: A system at equilibrium that is disturbed shifts to partly counteract the change.
Adding a species shifts away from it; reducing the volume shifts toward fewer moles of gas.
Raising the temperature shifts an endothermic reaction forward and changes K; adding a catalyst or an inert gas at constant volume causes no shift.

topics.title: Reaction Quotient and Le Châtelier's Principle
objectives: Justify an equilibrium shift by comparing Q with K.
knowledge: A change in concentration or pressure changes Q but not K; the system shifts until Q equals K again.
A temperature change changes K itself.
Justify shifts with Q vs K, not with rate language alone.

topics.title: Introduction to Solubility Equilibria
objectives: Write Ksp expressions and convert between Ksp and molar solubility.
knowledge: A slightly soluble salt in water reaches equilibrium with its ions; Ksp is the product of ion concentrations raised to their coefficients.
Molar solubility s is the moles of salt that dissolve per liter; for MX2, Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³.
Comparing Ksp directly works only for salts with the same ion ratio.

topics.title: Common-Ion Effect
objectives: Explain and calculate how a common ion lowers solubility.
knowledge: Adding an ion already in the equilibrium makes Q > Ksp, so more solid forms: solubility drops.
Ksp does not change; only the solubility does.

topics.title: Introduction to Acids and Bases
objectives: Relate pH, pOH, [H3O+] and [OH−] through the autoionization of water.
knowledge: Water ionizes slightly: Kw = [H3O+][OH−] = 1.0 × 10^-14 at 25 °C.
pH = −log[H3O+]; pOH = −log[OH−]; pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C.
A neutral solution has [H3O+] = [OH−]; Kw, and so neutral pH, changes with temperature.

topics.title: pH and pOH of Strong Acids and Bases
objectives: Calculate the pH of strong acid and strong base solutions, including mixtures.
knowledge: Strong acids and strong bases ionize completely in water, so [H3O+] or [OH−] comes straight from the concentration.
Know the common strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, HClO4, H2SO4 first proton) and strong bases (group 1 and heavy group 2 hydroxides).
When strong acid and strong base mix, find what is left over after neutralization, then the pH.

topics.title: Weak Acid and Base Equilibria
objectives: Calculate the pH of weak acid and weak base solutions with Ka or Kb.
knowledge: A weak acid is mostly un-ionized in water; Ka measures how far it ionizes, and pKa = −log Ka.
For a weak acid, [H3O+] ≈ √(Ka × C) when ionization is small.
Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair; percent ionization rises as a weak acid is diluted.

topics.title: Acid-Base Reactions and Buffers
objectives: Predict the products and pH of acid-base mixtures and recognize when a buffer forms.
knowledge: Strong acid + strong base gives a neutral solution at equivalence; a weak acid + strong base gives the conjugate base, so the solution is basic.
A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid) in similar amounts.
Partly neutralizing a weak acid with a strong base makes a buffer.

topics.title: Acid-Base Titrations
objectives: Read titration curves to find the equivalence point, half-equivalence point and pKa.
knowledge: A titration curve plots pH against volume of titrant; the steep rise centers on the equivalence point.
At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration, [HA] = [A−], so pH = pKa.
The pH at equivalence is 7 for strong-strong, above 7 for weak acid with strong base, below 7 for weak base with strong acid.
A polyprotic acid shows one equivalence point per ionizable proton.

topics.title: Molecular Structure of Acids and Bases
objectives: Explain relative acid strength from molecular structure and the stability of the conjugate base.
knowledge: An acid is stronger when its conjugate base is more stable: charge spread by resonance or pulled by electronegative atoms.
For oxyacids, more oxygen atoms or a more electronegative central atom makes the acid stronger.
Carboxylic acids are weak acids; amines are weak bases (they accept a proton on the nitrogen lone pair).

topics.title: pH and pKa
objectives: Compare pH and pKa to find which form of an acid predominates and choose an indicator.
knowledge: When pH < pKa, the protonated form predominates; when pH > pKa, the deprotonated form does; at pH = pKa they are equal.
An indicator changes color over about pKa ± 1, so choose one whose pKa is near the equivalence-point pH.

topics.title: Properties of Buffers
objectives: Explain at the particle level how a buffer resists pH change.
knowledge: Added strong acid reacts with the conjugate base; added strong base reacts with the weak acid, so few H3O+ or OH− ions remain free.
The buffer pH depends on the ratio of conjugate base to acid, not on their absolute amounts.
Diluting a buffer barely changes its pH.

topics.title: Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
objectives: Calculate buffer pH and buffer composition with the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.
knowledge: pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]), using base-10 log, not ln.
For a weak base buffer, use the pKa of the conjugate acid, not pKb.
To make a buffer of a chosen pH, pick an acid with pKa near that pH and set the ratio.

topics.title: Buffer Capacity
objectives: Compare buffer capacities and explain when a buffer is exhausted.
knowledge: Buffer capacity grows with the amounts of weak acid and conjugate base present.
A buffer resists additions of acid or base best when [A−] and [HA] are similar, and fails once one component is used up.

topics.title: pH and Solubility
objectives: Predict qualitatively how pH changes the solubility of a salt with a basic anion.
knowledge: A salt whose anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid becomes more soluble as pH falls, because H3O+ removes the anion and the equilibrium shifts toward dissolving.
Salts of anions from strong acids (Cl−, NO3−) are not affected by pH.
exclusions: Calculations of solubility as a function of pH are reported as not tested (needs-author: verify against the CED).

topics.title: Introduction to Entropy
objectives: Predict the sign of ΔS for a process with particle-level reasoning about how matter and energy disperse.
knowledge: Entropy measures how many ways (microstates) the particles and energy of a system can be arranged.
Entropy increases when matter spreads out (more gas particles, larger volume, solid to liquid to gas, dissolving) or energy spreads (higher temperature).
Explain entropy with dispersal of matter and energy, not with "disorder".

topics.title: Absolute Entropy and Entropy Change
objectives: Calculate ΔS° of a reaction from standard molar entropies.
knowledge: Every substance has a positive standard molar entropy S°; a perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy.
ΔS°rxn = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants), each times its coefficient; units are J/(mol·K).

topics.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability
objectives: Use ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° to decide whether a process is thermodynamically favored and at which temperatures.
knowledge: A process is thermodynamically favored when ΔG° < 0.
ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°; convert ΔS° from J to kJ (or ΔH° to J) and use kelvin.
The signs of ΔH° and ΔS° decide whether a process is favored at all, at none, at high or at low temperature.

topics.title: Thermodynamic and Kinetic Control
objectives: Explain why a thermodynamically favored process may not be observed at a measurable rate.
knowledge: A favored process with a very large activation energy can be too slow to observe: it is under kinetic control.
ΔG° says whether a process can go, not how fast.

topics.title: Free Energy and Equilibrium
objectives: Relate ΔG° to K with ΔG° = −RT ln K.
knowledge: ΔG° = −RT ln K, with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and T in kelvin.
ΔG° < 0 means K > 1 (products favored); ΔG° > 0 means K < 1.
When ΔG° is near zero, K is near 1 and both reactants and products are present in large amounts.

topics.title: Free Energy of Dissolution
objectives: Explain the enthalpy, entropy and free energy changes of dissolving a solid.
knowledge: Dissolving breaks solute-solute and solvent-solvent attractions (absorbs energy) and forms solute-solvent attractions (releases energy).
Dissolving usually raises entropy, though ordering of water around small, highly charged ions can lower it.
A solid dissolves readily when ΔG° of dissolution is negative.

topics.title: Coupled Reactions
objectives: Explain how coupling to a favored reaction drives an unfavored one.
knowledge: An unfavored reaction (ΔG° > 0) can proceed when coupled to a favored one so that the total ΔG° is negative.
Coupling needs a shared intermediate; ΔG° values of coupled steps add, and their K values multiply.
External energy (electric current, light) can also drive an unfavored process.

topics.title: Galvanic (Voltaic) and Electrolytic Cells
objectives: Describe the parts and electron flow of galvanic and electrolytic cells.
knowledge: In a galvanic cell a favored redox reaction produces an electric current; in an electrolytic cell a current drives an unfavored one.
Oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode; electrons flow through the wire from anode to cathode.
The salt bridge lets ions move to keep each half-cell neutral.
exclusions: Labeling electrodes as positive or negative is reported as not tested (needs-author: verify against the CED).

topics.title: Cell Potential and Free Energy
objectives: Calculate E°cell from half-reactions and relate it to ΔG°.
knowledge: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) using standard reduction potentials; a positive E°cell means a favored reaction.
E° is intensive: multiplying a half-reaction to balance electrons does not change its E°.
ΔG° = −nFE°, where n is moles of electrons transferred and F = 96,485 C/mol e−.

topics.title: Cell Potential Under Nonstandard Conditions
objectives: Predict how cell potential changes when concentrations change.
knowledge: When Q < 1, the cell potential is larger than E°; when Q > 1, it is smaller; at equilibrium the cell potential is zero.
The Nernst equation, E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, describes this; the exam emphasizes reasoning about direction.
A concentration cell has the same half-reaction on both sides and runs on a concentration difference.
exclusions: Quantitative Nernst calculations are reported as de-emphasized (needs-author: verify against the CED).

topics.title: Electrolysis and Faraday's Law
objectives: Calculate the amount of substance produced or used in electrolysis from current and time.
knowledge: Charge = current × time (q = It); charge ÷ F gives moles of electrons.
Moles of electrons and the half-reaction give moles, then mass, of the substance plated or produced.

skillsTopics.title: Units and Dimensional Analysis
objectives: Carry units through every calculation and convert between them with conversion factors.
knowledge: Every measured quantity is a number with a unit; the unit is part of the answer.
Metric prefixes (giga to pico) scale a unit by powers of ten; kilo is 10^3, milli 10^-3, micro 10^-6, nano 10^-9.
A conversion factor is a ratio equal to one, so multiplying by it changes the unit, not the quantity.
Temperature in kelvin is the Celsius temperature plus 273.15; gas and thermodynamics equations need kelvin.
Density is mass divided by volume.

skillsTopics.title: Exponents
objectives: Use the rules of exponents to multiply, divide and raise powers.
knowledge: An exponent says how many times a base is multiplied by itself; a negative exponent means one over the power.
Multiplying powers of the same base adds exponents; dividing subtracts them; a power of a power multiplies them.
A fractional exponent is a root: x^(1/2) is the square root of x.

skillsTopics.title: Scientific Notation
objectives: Write, read and calculate with numbers in scientific notation.
knowledge: Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 to less than 10 times a power of ten.
To multiply, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents; to divide, divide and subtract.
A calculator entry such as 6.022E23 means 6.022 × 10^23.
An order of magnitude is a factor of ten; comparing exponents compares sizes quickly.

skillsTopics.title: Significant Figures
objectives: Report a calculated value with the number of significant figures the data support.
knowledge: Significant figures are the digits a measurement actually knows, plus one estimated digit.
Nonzero digits and zeros between them count; leading zeros never count; trailing zeros count when there is a decimal point.
Multiplying or dividing: keep as many significant figures as the least precise factor.
Adding or subtracting: keep as many decimal places as the least precise term.
For a logarithm such as pH, the number of decimal places equals the significant figures of the concentration.
Exact numbers (counted items, defined conversions) do not limit significant figures.

skillsTopics.title: Logarithms
objectives: Use base-10 and natural logarithms and their inverses in chemistry equations.
knowledge: The base-10 logarithm of a number is the power of ten that gives the number: log(1000) = 3.
The natural logarithm (ln) uses base e; ln x = 2.303 log x.
log(ab) = log a + log b and log(a/b) = log a − log b; log(10^x) = x.
The inverse of log is 10^x; the inverse of ln is e^x.
Mixing up ln and log is one of the most common calculation errors on the exam.
